This was explicitly discounted in the original design.  As someone who has maintained things that supported arbitrary includes, maintenance is a nightmare.

For example, if you have a common #include, and you make an edit to it, are we going to require that all board variants be tested?  How do we stage that?


Also keep in mind that EM files are supposed to be self contained so that they're not tied to a specific firmware revision (and generally have infinite backward compatibility).

Adding this new feature breaks that property, and makes things like single image systems not possible.

> For example, if you have a common #include, and you make an edit to it, are we going to require that all board variants be tested? How do we stage that?

I think it would depend on the property and who owns those configurations.

And some people do have hardware CI and are capable to test multiple boards in an automated way.

In general this feature works in both directions for maximum flexibility 😎
The configuration can be de-duplicated but also inlined as needed. If there is the need to change a property but no way to test the other variants, the changed property goes into the ```Override``` property or the whole record is simply inlined and then changed 👍

> Also keep in mind that EM files are supposed to be self contained so that they're not tied to a specific firmware revision (and generally have infinite backward compatibility).

Would you prefer this to be a compile-time feature? That way there would then only be full configuration files on the BMC. It may even work better with the ```compatible-hardware``` proposal then, since there will be no dangling .record.json files.

> > For example, if you have a common #include, and you make an edit to it, are we going to require that all board variants be tested? How do we stage that?
> 
> I think it would depend on the property and who owns those configurations.

OpenBMC as a whole maintains the configurations.  There's not one "owner".

> 
> And some people do have hardware CI and are capable to test multiple boards in an automated way.

And that's wonderful for those folks.  We should encourage that more, but I don't see that reported to gerrit CI on EM commits, so the point still stands.

> 
> In general this feature works in both directions for maximum flexibility 😎
> The configuration can be de-duplicated but also inlined as needed. If there is the need to change a property but no way to test the other variants, the changed property goes into the ```Override``` property or the whole record is simply inlined and then changed 👍
> 
> > Also keep in mind that EM files are supposed to be self contained so that they're not tied to a specific firmware revision (and generally have infinite backward compatibility).
> 
> Would you prefer this to be a compile-time feature? That way there would then only be full configuration files on the BMC. It may even work better with the ```compatible-hardware``` proposal then, since there will be no dangling .record.json files.

I'm not sure how moving it to compile time solves the issue.  now folks need to do a full compile anytime they want to make an individual change to something with a #include in it?  That seems worse.  it's pretty common you make an edit to a config live on system, or SCP a config to a system and restart the reactors.  That ability gets lost if the files now require being a template.

With that said, I think we can build something that gets what you want (some level of confidence that files remain the same).  See my comment on the other commit.

> OpenBMC as a whole maintains the configurations. There's not one "owner".

It's impossible to fully test configurations if you do not have the board.
Best you can do is some light maintenance, refactoring and migration.

Most boards do not even have schematics online, so any changes of actual configuration records like Bus, Address, Thresholds, Scale factors, ... will be guesswork at best for anyone without the access.

If you prevent those contributing the configuration from owning it, it will only encourage them to keep those downstream, which is not in the interests of this project.

> I'm not sure how moving it to compile time solves the issue. now folks need to do a full compile anytime they want to make an individual change to something with a #include in it? That seems worse. it's pretty common you make an edit to a config live on system, or SCP a config to a system and restart the reactors.

If the include feature is moved to compile-time, the configs on the BMC will be complete. So there is no issue to edit them directly.

If the edit is done in EM repository, processing includes for a single configuration might take less than one second. I don't see why a 'full compile' would be needed there?

> That ability gets lost if the files now require being a template.

If you do not want to use that feature, you don't have to. It's an opt-in feature for people maintaining multiple boards to deduplicate their configuration.

If it turns out no one needs such a feature or people do not use it, we can drop the feature after some time.

> It's impossible to fully test configurations if you do not have the board.
> ....will be guesswork

Yep.... exactly, so to keep things stable, the duplication helps because you can operate only on the boards that you have access to when you're testing.

> If you prevent those contributing the configuration from owning it

This confuses me.  How does #includes prevent the ownership of the config files?  In my mind it hinders, because you need both ownership of the #include file (which might be owned by a company that doesn't prioritize reviewing/testing you change) and the config file.  In the current model, you could make an asset tag change, and write a config file that ONLY recognizes one board in isolation, so we can test things as needed.


> If you do not want to use that feature, you don't have to.

The problem here is there is no "you" in open source.  Lots of folks contribute configs for boards then move on to other things.  If SOME people use an include feature, then the next person to make improvements faces the issue that they have to do a major refactor to make a minor change on their board, because they probably don't have access to all other boards.

> Yep.... exactly, so to keep things stable, the duplication helps because you can operate only on the boards that you have access to when you're testing.

In the newest revision, the file which is generated from the template is part of the EM source tree. The script can then run as part of CI to ensure there is no diff in the tree.

So all configurations which are changed as part of a change to an included file will show up in the review 😎

>  If SOME people use an include feature, then the next person to make improvements faces the issue that they have to do a major refactor to make a minor change on their board, because they probably don't have access to all other boards.

As i already said, the ```Override``` feature is intended to make minor changes on top of an included Exposes record. If many properties are changed, it might make sense to inline that record. With the newest revision, it is very easy to just take the fully expanded record and inline it into the template, since it's already part of the source tree. So there is no 'major refactor' required 👍
Resolved this since most concerns should be addressed by newest revision and no further comment since 1 month.

Overall I'm not in support of this type of feature, as it defeats some of the purpose of having runtime-read config files in the first place, and complicates the maintenance burden for any common files.  If configs are truly common enough that we can pick defaults, then we shouldn't have a configuration at all, just add it as a feature in code that can be selected with a single property or type.

FWIW, the predecessor to entity manager implemented this feature, and it needed to be completely undone due to the maintenance issues around minor changes to a single platform or component needing major refactors due to the files being created originally as "common".

If we want to talk through guard rails to prevent the above issues, I'm happy to discuss further.

> complicates the maintenance burden for any common files

Yes, but it also allows to easily introduce changes across multiple board variants and keep things in sync. Imagine you have some exposes records which are already part of multiple configs and do not differ much.

Having a way to deduplicate that can help to avoid the configurations drifting apart.

## realistic use-case for shared configuration records

Some properties which i would like to keep in sync between boards and board variants:

- Thresholds for specific components (the component is the same, just different address and bus and living on a different board)

- Name property (VBAT, CPU_TEMP, ... ) can often be the same. Since it is the same component, just on a different board.

- Type property

## dealing with changes which cannot be validated for all boards

> due to the maintenance issues around minor changes to a single platform or component needing major refactors due to the files being created originally as "common".

If there is a change needed for a configuration which does not apply to all variants or cannot be validated for all of them, it can go in ```Override``` property. If there are too many ```Override``` properties, there is no need to include and the whole record can be inlined.

## proposed guardrails for review of the usage of the feature

- no sharing common configuration records (for baseboards) across OEMs
- good to share configuration records for slightly different board variants from same OEM
- if there are too many ```Override``` properties on an included record, the record can be inlined.

> > complicates the maintenance burden for any common files
> 
> Yes, but it also allows to easily introduce changes across multiple board variants and keep things in sync.

Right, and this is an anti pattern because of the testing requirement.  If you have one config that's used on 8 boards, it's fairly unlikely you actually tested all 8 boards with your commit.  Having them separate lets the changes be made as the boards are tested, one at a time, or in chunks (one lead, others follow once stable).

> Thresholds for specific components

If this is truly common, just put it in the application code.  FWIW, there are many cases where systems "start" with common thresholds, then as more data is available, transition to more specific thresholds.  Keeping them separate prevents bugs and makes code scope a lot more reviewable so we're not breaking working systems when we piece apart a config.

> If there is a change needed for a configuration which does not apply to all variants or cannot be validated for all of them, it can go in Override property.

Right, so now we've cause a problem, then needed to invent new code to solve the problem.  Lets just not create the problem in the first place.

> no sharing common configuration records (for baseboards) across OEMs

This would defeat most of your patches, right?  Most of the shared config is cross odm?

> if there are too many Override properties on an included record, the record can be inlined.

"too many" is too subjective for me.  If the override is required at all, the config should be rolled out.


The above guard rails don't solve the issues around review velocity, or blast radius.
What if we did something like this as an annotation:

{
   "Property1": "Value"
   "Type" "MyType"
   "@FromTemplate": "template_name.json"
}

then in the template_name.json

{
   "Property1": "Value",
   "Type: "Mytype",
}

Then have warnings (maybe build errors) when a config deviates from the template.  This has a couple good properties compared to what's proposed in this patch, we can have our templates, but we still keep two important development properties:

1. Em files and code reviews are reviewable easily for "What systems does this effect", because template changes will still show in all the systems they effect.
2. EM files continue to be self contained, so we keep the use case of "SCP a config file to a system to test a config" that is very common in development.

> Right, and this is an anti pattern because of the testing requirement. If you have one config that's used on 8 boards, it's fairly unlikely you actually tested all 8 boards with your commit. Having them separate lets the changes be made as the boards are tested, one at a time, or in chunks (one lead, others follow once stable).

That's what the ```Override``` feature is meant for. To be able to share configuration and introduce some small differences.


> If this is truly common, just put it in the application code. FWIW, there are many cases where systems "start" with common thresholds, then as more data is available, transition to more specific thresholds. Keeping them separate prevents bugs and makes code scope a lot more reviewable so we're not breaking working systems when we piece apart a config.

Disagree. Thresholds should come from the configuration. If you have an ADC, Temperature or Air flow sensor, what is a sensible default Threshold? 

I also don't think that Thresholds should just change at runtime without any user actions. When do Thresholds 'transition' to be more specific? Why can't they be right from the start?

> "too many" is too subjective for me. If the override is required at all, the config should be rolled out.

If you have 3 baseboard temperature sensors which are only different in their i2c bus and address, that should not need to be duplicated.

If you have 2 board variants which share a common component, that should not have to be duplicated across 2 configs. Especially if the variants are functionally equivalent and only vary by small details like component manufacturer.

And having an array of EM configs in a single file does **not** solve the duplication issue.
